Origine.title: The Origins of Carnet de Vie
Origine.subtitle: Preserve heartfelt memories today, so that one day your child can embrace where they come from and remain free to become who they are.

1.step: 1. THE OBSERVATION AND THE FOUNDING IDEA
1.title: Preserving what a photograph cannot capture
1.p1: We have all felt that emotion when rediscovering a trace of our childhood: a photo, a note, a drawing, a memory that seems to whisper: You mattered, you were loved, you were here.
1.p2: Today, we take thousands of photos and videos. But children's words, first experiences, tender gestures, emotions and the perspectives of those who were there become scattered.
1.p3: Carnet de Vie grew from this simple insight: to preserve, from the wish for a child to their 18th birthday, accounts of what was experienced, felt and shared alongside them.
1.quote: We cannot hold back time, but we can preserve some of its traces.

2.title: Understanding to support them better
2.p1: At every age, a child develops in three main areas: physical, emotional and cognitive. Their needs, their emotions and the challenges they face change as they grow.
2.p2: The Parenting Guide offers clear, practical guidance, informed by the insights of paediatricians, psychologists, psychiatrists and other professionals recognised in their fields.
2.p3: It does not seek to impose a parenting model, but to help each parent understand what their child is going through, step back and find their own answers, in line with their values.
2.quote: Guidance to light your path, never to choose for you.

3.title: Words to pass on with kindness
3.p1: A child grows up surrounded by bonds, words, caring eyes and the presence of others. Parents, grandparents, brothers, sisters and loved ones can each pass on a part of their story.
3.p2: Because a true story can also include difficult moments, an artificial intelligence tool inspired by the principles of Nonviolent Communication (NVC) helps people put their accounts into words, so that these do not become a space for judgement, blame or tensions.
3.quote: Carnet de Vie does not set a story in stone. It simply ensures that it is not lost and is passed on with respect and kindness.

4.step: 4. PASSING IT ON: A RITUAL ACROSS GENERATIONS?
4.title: An act of love at 18.
4.p1: At 18, the Carnet is passed on to the child, now a young adult, as an act of love.
4.p2: It allows them to make a story their own, helping them understand the journey they have taken and what has shaped them.
4.p3: The Carnet now belongs to them: they can embrace this story — without having to repair it — give it their own meaning and freely continue their own, remaining free to become themselves.
4.quote: Two voices. One shared commitment: to pass on without confining, to receive without having to repair.

Origine.closingQuote: “Carnet de Vie is more than a family photo album. It is a structured foundation for identity that turns the past into energy for growth.”
Origine.closingAuthor: Luc and Sylvie M. de Barnier

About.bannerAlt: Sylvie and Luc - Who we are
About.title: Who are we?
About.subtitle:
We are parents, supporters and observers of life: psychologists, psychiatrists, paediatricians, midwives, coaches… a team with complementary talents to support you

But above all, we are people who, over the years, have seen how much the words and gestures directed towards a child can matter throughout their life.

1.title: Sylvie de Barnier
1.p1: Sylvie de Barnier has been a clinical psychologist for more than thirty-five years. She supports adults, teenagers, children and families.
1.p2: Over the years, she has witnessed profound changes in our society and in parenting: parents today are more involved, more attentive and more aware of what they pass on. But they also face greater pressure, caught between wanting to do well, the demands of daily life and an ideal that can be difficult to reach.
1.quote: Supporting parents also means helping them find their own way of being parents.

2.title: Luc M. de Barnier
2.p1: Luc M. de Barnier is a life coach and psychotherapist. He pays particular attention to the quality of communication within families, couples and sibling relationships, where everyday bonds, tensions and balances take shape.
2.p2: His approach gives a central place to listening, respecting each person and communicating in a way that allows people to express their experiences without hurting others.
2.quote: The quality of a relationship is also built through the way we speak to one another.

3.title: A shared perspective
3.p1: Through their work, Sylvie and Luc have seen reference points change, family dynamics shift, separations become more common and new blended families form.
3.p2: Above all, they have met parents who search, who doubt and who, despite their vulnerabilities and everyday difficulties, do their best for their child.
3.p3: Carnet de Vie was born from this shared perspective: to guide, support and pass on, without demands or an imposed model.
3.quote: There is no perfect parent. There are parents finding their way.

4.title: A team by your side
4.p1: Carnet de Vie does not rely on a single approach.
4.p2: Sylvie and Luc work with professionals in childhood, adolescence and family life: paediatricians, gynaecologists, family doctors, psychiatrists, primary school teachers and psychologists.
4.p3: Their complementary perspectives address children's development in its physical, psychological, emotional, cognitive, relational and family dimensions.
4.quote: A child grows in many dimensions. Supporting them calls for different perspectives.

About.closingQuote: Carnet de Vie: a record of memories for the child. A gift passed on by those who love them.
About.closingAuthor: Luc and Sylvie M. de Barnier

Guide.title: The Parenting Guide
Guide.tagline: Valuable guidance for the big challenges of everyday life
Guide.subtitle:
Clear, practical insights into children's physical, emotional and cognitive development,

provided by recognised professionals in childhood and adolescence.

1.title: Development as a whole
1.p1: At every age, children develop in three main areas: physical, emotional and cognitive. The Parenting Guide offers age-appropriate guidance to help you understand these changes and their possible effects on everyday life.
1.quote: Growing up means developing on several levels, sometimes at different paces.

2.step: 2. SHEDDING LIGHT ON THE BIG QUESTIONS
2.title: Everyday challenges
2.p1: Sleep, food, emotions, independence, boundaries, screens, school, relationships, puberty, adolescence... Concerns change as children grow.
2.p2: The Guide offers accessible, practical insights to help you find your footing when difficulties arise.
2.quote: Some worries already begin to ease when we understand more clearly what is happening.

3.title: A recognised team
3.p1: Paediatricians, psychologists, psychiatrists, gynaecologists, family doctors, teachers and other specialists share insights from their areas of expertise.
3.p2: The Guide does not replace a professional. It helps you understand a situation, find your bearings and, when necessary, identify whom to turn to.
3.quote: Combining perspectives can help us see our concerns in a different light.

4.title: Kind and supportive guidance
4.p1: Carnet de Vie does not seek to promote a single parenting model or tell parents how they should raise their child.
4.p2: The Guide offers reference points to help them step back, reflect and find a response suited to their child, their family and their values.
4.quote: Guidance to light your path, never to choose for you.

Guide.closingQuote: Being a parent does not mean knowing everything. It also means seeking the right guidance when you need it.
Guide.closingAuthor: Luc and Sylvie M. de Barnier

Communication.title: Compassionate Communication
Communication.tagline: Words to understand each other, bonds to grow
Communication.subtitle:
An invitation to listen, to express your emotions and to welcome those of others, inspired by Nonviolent Communication and the ESPERE® method.

Simple guidance for nurturing authentic, respectful and caring relationships within the family.

1.title: Communicating to meet each other better
1.p1: Communicating is not just about exchanging words. It is also about trying to understand what each person is going through, feeling and trying to express, sometimes clumsily.
1.p2: In the parent–child relationship, emotions, expectations and misunderstandings can make dialogue difficult. Compassion invites us to welcome what is being lived without giving up on expressing our own needs and limits.
1.p3: Carnet de Vie offers another way of talking and listening to each other, where everyone can find their place without having to agree on everything.
1.quote: Compassion does not mean accepting everything, but recognising each person in what they are going through.

2.title: Guidance, not an imposed method
2.p1: Our approach draws in particular on Nonviolent Communication (NVC), developed by Marshall Rosenberg, which invites us to distinguish facts from judgements, to recognise emotions and needs, and to make requests rather than demands.
2.p2: It is also enriched by Jacques Salomé's ESPERE® method, which gives a central place to the quality of the relationship, to each person's responsibility in exchanges and to respect for differences.
2.p3: Carnet de Vie does not reproduce any of these methods to the letter. It draws on their spirit to offer simple guidance, suited to family life and to passing things on.
2.quote: Drawing on several perspectives to find your own way of relating to others.

3.title: Listen, express, respect
3.p1: A child may express fear through anger, sadness through silence or a need for independence through defiance. Behind a behaviour, there is sometimes something asking to be heard.
3.p2: Compassionate Communication invites parents to step back, to tell what they observe apart from what they interpret, and to speak of their own feelings rather than defining the other person's.
3.p3: It also makes it possible to set limits, express disagreement and work through conflict without seeking to make anyone feel guilty or to belittle them.
3.quote: Listen without disappearing, stand your ground without hurting, guide without imposing.

4.title: Finding the words to pass on
4.p1: Writing to your child is not always easy. Some memories are happy, others more sensitive. Emotions, regrets or expectations can slip into the words you wish to leave them.
4.p2: When the parent wishes, an artificial intelligence tool helps them phrase their entries. It can suggest a clearer, more respectful wording, without erasing the emotions or changing the meaning of what was lived.
4.p3: The parent always remains free to keep, change or decline its suggestions. The aim is not to embellish the story, but to let it be passed on without placing the weight of the adult's emotions on the child.
4.quote: Preserving the truth of what was lived, with words that leave the other free to receive it.

Communication.closingQuote: Communicating with compassion is not always about finding the right words. Above all, it is about seeking to understand the other without giving up on being yourself.
Communication.closingAuthor: Luc and Sylvie M. de Barnier

Chemin.title: The Life Journey
Chemin.description: From the wish for a child to their 18th birthday, Carnet de Vie supports every stage of their development and helps you preserve its essential traces.
Chemin.stagesLabel: The stages of the Life Journey
Chemin.momentsLabel: Special moments on the Life Journey

1.title: Developing step by step
1.p1: For each age group, an overview of how children grow helps you better understand their development and their personality at that time.
1.quote: Growing up means constantly changing while gradually building who we are.

2.title: Keeping a record of what matters
2.p1: Questions invite you to clarify how you feel at each stage of your child's life and help you identify what you want to gather from them and pass on in their Carnet de Vie.
2.quote: A few questions can sometimes bring to light what we would not want to forget.

3.title: Moments out of time
3.p1: Bonding rituals suited to each stage of your child's life help you create and nurture a secure bond with them.
3.quote: A repeated ritual can become one of childhood's most precious memories.

4.title: Guidance that reassures
4.p1: Essential, carefully selected links about childhood and adolescence help you find answers to your questions, doubts and concerns, offering reassurance and guidance.
4.quote: Understanding what a child is going through often helps us support them better.

Chemin.closingQuote: Every age brings changes, discoveries and challenges. Every stage leaves something to preserve.
Chemin.closingAuthor: Luc and Sylvie M. de Barnier

0.title:
Welcome to

their Carnet de Vie

items.1: a warm, joyful space to return to each day, like a comforting companion for parents,
items.2: empathetic, science-based guidance on child development,
items.3: emotional support for parents or couples,
items.4: a structured, caring family memory, passed on to the child at 18.

0.quote:
Carnet de Vie does not set a story in stone.

It simply ensures that it is not lost in a fast-moving world that sometimes leaves little room for what matters most.

p.1: Between four and five, something becomes more firmly established. Children no longer simply imagine the world: they want to act upon it.
p.2: Try. Succeed. Show. Children run faster, build higher, take greater care and try to finish what they have started. Above all, they want to share this experience: ‘Look what I’ve done.’
p.3: The adult’s gaze becomes a source of inner support. Through it, children begin to feel that what they do matters, that their actions have value and that they have a place among others.
p.4: A drawing shown several times, a construction that must not be taken apart, a performance repeated over and over can carry an unspoken question: ‘Does what I do have value to you?’

2.label: Guidance to support them
2.title: Guidance to support them
2.intro: Between four and five, children want to act independently, succeed and be recognised. A sense of competence builds confidence, while groups and friendships become more important. Adults encourage effort without placing excessive pressure on the result.
2.quote: Emotional security remains essential to daring to try.
2.more: → Explore further: {count} insights from the Parenting Guide

3.label: Invitations to share
3.title: Invitations to share
3.lead: I can respond to just one invitation. They are simply signposts, a guide. A sentence is enough. A word, a photo or a video too. Or I can come back later.

4.label: Bonding ritual
4.title: The drawn portrait
4.subtitle: The child draws a character that represents them.

p.1: At this age, drawings do more than depict things. They also allow children to express something of themselves.
p.2: The way children draw themselves, where others are placed, the colours chosen, the details omitted or repeated sometimes tell us something about their way of being in the world.
p.3: I do not interpret too quickly. I stay curious. Available.
p.4: Sometimes I photograph a drawing. Not to accumulate memories. But to show the child that what they create matters.

4.quote: Growing up also means feeling that what we bring to the world has a place in the eyes of those we love.
4.invite: We invite you to film or photograph this moment and add it to Carnet de Vie.

5.label: Precious moments
5.title: What I choose to keep from this year

items.6: A moment when the child went beyond their limits.
items.7: Or simply a moment I do not want to forget.

5.quote:
I leave our precious moments here,

to give them to you one day and say thank you.

options.1: likes to finish what has been started
options.5: quickly gives up when facing difficulty

1.quote: Growing up means discovering what you feel capable of.

3.title: 3. When facing failure or frustration, the child:
3.quote: Learning also means working through disappointment.

options.2: stays close to a small group of friends
options.3: looks for their place in the group

5.title: 5. In role play, the child:

options.6: re-enacts experiences from school or elsewhere

5.quote: Play becomes a space for exploring relationships.

6.title: 6. When making sense of time, the child:

options.4: asks many questions about the future

6.quote: A sense of time slowly begins to take shape.

7.title: 7. The bond between us feels:

options.5: nurtured by their need to see me as a role model

7.quote: Children want to grow without losing the connection.

8.title: 8. When the child shows something they have made:

options.4: seems disappointed if I do not notice

8.quote: A parent's attention remains deeply formative.

10.title: 10. What particularly stands out to me at the moment:
10.quote: The child becomes more capable. I remain a source of guidance.

evolution.title: Physical, emotional and cognitive development (4–5 years)
evolution.summary: The major changes in the body, thinking, language and emotions.

p.1: Between four and five, development becomes more stable. The body becomes more coordinated and movements more precise. Children run, jump and climb with greater confidence.
p.2: Fine motor skills also develop: cutting, drawing, assembling and handling objects become easier.
p.3: Cognitively, thinking begins to organise actions more effectively. Children understand more of the connections between situations, can anticipate certain steps and follow more complex instructions.
p.4: Language becomes a real tool for thinking and sharing: children tell stories, explain, ask questions and imagine.
p.5: Something also becomes more refined emotionally. Emotions are easier to identify, but remain strongly influenced by the context and the responses of others.
p.6: Feeling capable becomes essential. Adult support plays a profound part in building self-esteem.

points.1: The body and its movements become more precise.
points.2: Thinking begins to organise and anticipate actions more effectively.
points.3: Language becomes a tool for telling stories, explaining and thinking.
points.4: A sense of competence becomes important.
points.5: An adult's caring attention profoundly supports a child's confidence.

estime.title: Self-esteem or self-confidence?
estime.summary: Understanding the difference between “I can do it” and “I matter”.

p.1: At this age, children are developing both self-confidence and self-esteem.
p.2: Self-confidence relates to what children believe they can do: “I am capable.” Completing a task, overcoming a challenge or learning something new nurtures it.
p.3: Self-esteem concerns a sense of personal worth: “I matter.” That worth remains even when a child fails or has doubts.
p.4: At this age, the two can still become confused. Success can make children feel “strong”, while failure can make them feel worth less.
p.5: The adult’s role is therefore essential: valuing effort, recognising progress and offering support without reducing the child to their performance.

points.1: Self-confidence concerns what children feel capable of doing.
points.2: Self-esteem concerns the feeling of having worth.
points.3: Success and personal worth can still easily become confused.
points.4: Valuing effort and progress avoids defining children by the result.
points.5: Children need to feel that their worth remains, even when an attempt fails.

phrases.title: The 5 foundational phrases
phrases.summary: Words and gestures that can support inner security.

p.1: Certain phrases can offer lasting support for a sense of inner security. They are not magic: their strength comes from the relationship and their consistency with actions.
p.2: “I love you just as you are.”
p.7: The child learns without excessive fear of failure.
p.8: “I am here if you need me.”
p.11: The child feels that their presence matters.
p.12: Words do not replace gestures, caring attention, availability or physical affection. They accompany them. Together, they gradually build an inner foundation that children can rely on.

points.1: Words gain their value when they are consistent with the relationship.
points.2: Children need to be loved regardless of their achievements.
points.3: Encouraging children to try builds a stronger foundation than demanding success.
points.4: Being allowed to make mistakes protects the joy of learning.
points.5: Words, gestures, caring attention and affection work together to build inner security.

dessin.title: How drawing develops (3–5 years)
dessin.summary: Drawing as a language and a meaningful trace of the inner world.

p.1: Between three and five, drawing changes profoundly. At first, children mainly draw for the pleasure of movement: the hand moves, a line appears, and meaning may come afterwards.
p.2: Around three to four, the “tadpole person” often appears: a head with arms and legs, without a distinct body. This is not a mistake, but a representation consistent with how the child perceives a person at that stage.
p.3: Around four to five, figures become more complete. Details appear: eyes, clothes, hair, hands. The space on the page also begins to take shape: ground at the bottom, sky at the top, a house, a family, a sun.
p.4: Drawing gradually becomes a scene from the child's inner world. It is not about judging artistic performance. Drawing is a language.
p.5: Some features may sometimes reflect what a child is experiencing, but parents do not need to interpret them too quickly. They can look, listen and accept. Describe before asking questions. Let the child explain what they have drawn.
p.6: Photographing some drawings can be a gentle way of recognising the value of what is being expressed.

points.1: Drawing develops alongside a child's representation of the world.
points.2: It is a language as much as a creation.
points.3: There is no need to aim for artistic achievement.
points.4: It is better to let children talk about their drawings than to interpret them too quickly.
points.5: Keeping some creations acknowledges the value of what is expressed.

closing.1: Children gradually build their place in the world.
